newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Ivory Coast plans second-tier coffee price.
newsitem.headline: Ivory Coast plans second-tier coffee price.

text.p: Ivory Coast is planning a second-tier farmgate price as a guideline for marketing large volumes of poor quality beans, industry sources said on Tuesday.
"(The price) is not out yet so the final percentage adjustment is not clear," said one source. "We thought it would be announced last week."
Ivory Coast opened its 1996/97 season with a single guide farmgate robusta coffee price of 200 CFA per kilo, down from last year's 495 CFA in response to lower world prices.
Quality problems have since slowed grading at villages and ports. Quality inspectors had predicted exports of 150,000 tonnes, despite an official harvest forecast of 230,000.
Asked if the sub-grade price adjustment would be published next week, a source close to the Caistab coffee marketing board said, "I hope so."
Buyers said farmers in some areas had harvested beans too quickly in an attempt to be among the first to sell, stored beans in poor conditions and paid little attention to sorting.
Farmers' representatives said farmers had been paid as little as 300 CFA per kilo because of low world prices in late 1996 and as a result of quality problems in some areas.
Buying agents said exporters were making large price adjustments for quality at port and not advancing enough bank finance.
Industry buyers said a second-tier price was needed.
"An official price will make everyone's position in the marketing price chain a lot clearer," said one exporter.
"We are paying buyers one official green coffee price for grades one to four, but there are a lot of breakages and black beans that fall outside the scale," said another.
Exporters with enough finance to start buying in January had concentrated on higher grades.
A rally by world coffee prices in early 1997 had since sparked off renewed buying activity, with exporters citing good sales opportunities for sub-grades.
Ivory Coast's coffee was harvested earlier than usual this year but marketing has been slightly delayed as buyers concentrated on a large cocoa harvest.
Port stocks of coffee were around 100,000 tonnes by March 16 as exports lagged behind arrivals of around 150,000.
